title: Relations and functions
subject: Mathematics
summary: A relation is a set of ordered pairs; a function is a relation in which every input has exactly one output.
points: A function is one-one (injective) if different inputs never share an output, and onto (surjective) if every codomain element is used.
Composition means applying one function after another: (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)).
An inverse function exists only when the function is both one-one and onto.
Relations can be reflexive, symmetric and transitive; a relation with all three is an equivalence relation.

formulas.name: Number of relations
formulas.expr: 2^(mn) from a set of m elements to one of n elements

example: f(x) = 2x + 3 is one-one and onto on the reals, so f⁻¹(x) = (x − 3)/2.
mistakes: Calling any relation a function.
Assuming every function has an inverse.

title: Inverse trigonometric functions
subject: Mathematics
summary: Inverse trigonometric functions undo the trigonometric ratios, and they are defined only on restricted domains so that each value is unique.
points: Principal value branches are fixed by convention: sin⁻¹ has range [−π/2, π/2], cos⁻¹ has [0, π], tan⁻¹ has (−π/2, π/2).
sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2 for values in the domain.
Composing a trigonometric function with its inverse needs care because the inverse returns only the principal value.

formulas.name: Sum formula
formulas.expr: tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)), xy < 1

example: sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6, not 5π/6, because only the principal branch is reported.
mistakes: Writing sin⁻¹x as 1/sin x.
Ignoring the principal-value range.

title: Continuity and differentiability
subject: Mathematics
summary: A function is continuous at a point when its limit equals its value there, and differentiable when that limit of the difference quotient exists.
points: Continuity at x = a needs the left limit, right limit and f(a) all to be equal.
Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does not imply differentiability (for example |x| at 0).
The chain rule, product rule and quotient rule build derivatives of composite functions.
Rolle's and Lagrange's mean value theorems connect average and instantaneous rates of change.

formulas.name: Lagrange MVT
formulas.expr: f′(c) = [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a) for some c in (a, b)

example: f(x) = |x| is continuous everywhere but has no derivative at x = 0 because the left and right slopes are −1 and +1.
mistakes: Assuming continuity guarantees differentiability.
Forgetting to check both one-sided limits.

title: Applications of derivatives
subject: Mathematics
summary: Derivatives measure rates of change, give the slope of a tangent, and locate maxima and minima of a function.
points: If f′(x) > 0 on an interval the function increases there; if f′(x) < 0 it decreases.
At a stationary point f′(x) = 0; the sign change of f′ decides maximum, minimum or neither.
The second derivative test uses f″(x): negative gives a local maximum, positive a local minimum.
Real problems (cost, area, volume, speed) are solved by writing a function of one variable and optimising it.
example: A square sheet of side 12 cm has corners cut to make an open box of side x; volume V = x(12 − 2x)² is largest at x = 2 cm.
mistakes: Testing only f′(x) = 0 without checking the sign change.
Optimising without stating the domain of the variable.

title: Application of integrals (areas)
subject: Mathematics
summary: A definite integral gives the area between a curve and an axis, and between two curves it gives the area enclosed between them.
points: Area under y = f(x) from a to b is ∫f(x)dx when the curve lies above the x-axis.
Area between two curves is ∫[upper − lower]dx over the interval where they cross.
Sketch the region first: the limits of integration come from the points where the curves meet the axes or each other.

formulas.name: Area between curves
formulas.expr: A = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x) − g(x)] dx, f above g

example: The area enclosed by y = x², x = 0, x = 2 and the x-axis is ∫₀²x²dx = 8/3 square units.
mistakes: Ignoring the part of the region below the x-axis.
Using the wrong upper and lower function.

title: Linear inequalities
subject: Mathematics
summary: A linear inequality compares a linear expression with a number or another expression, and its solution is a range of values rather than a single value.
points: Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides keeps the inequality direction.
Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign.
Two-variable inequalities describe half-planes, and a system of them describes a feasible region.
Solutions are written as intervals or shown on a number line.

formulas.name: Interval notation
formulas.expr: a ≤ x ≤ b is written [a, b]

example: 3x − 4 < 8 gives 3x < 12, so x < 4, written as (−∞, 4).
mistakes: Forgetting to flip the sign when dividing by a negative.
Including the boundary point when the inequality is strict.

title: Linear programming
subject: Mathematics
summary: Linear programming finds the largest or smallest value of a linear objective function subject to linear constraints.
points: Constraints are written as linear inequalities and their common region is the feasible region.
The optimal value of a linear objective on a bounded feasible region occurs at a corner (vertex) of that region.
Unbounded regions need the objective checked along the open directions before a maximum or minimum is claimed.
Real problems are translated into variables, constraints and an objective before solving.

formulas.name: Objective
formulas.expr: Maximise or minimise Z = ax + by

formulas.name: Corner point method
formulas.expr: Z is evaluated at each vertex of the feasible region

example: Maximise Z = 3x + 2y subject to x + y ≤ 4, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0: vertices give Z = 12 at (4, 0).
mistakes: Missing a constraint when drawing the region.
Assuming an optimum exists when the region is unbounded.

title: Three dimensional geometry
subject: Mathematics
summary: Three dimensional geometry describes points, lines and planes using coordinates and direction ratios in space.
points: Direction cosines of a line are the cosines of the angles it makes with the x, y and z axes, and their squares add to 1.
A line is fixed by a point and a direction; a plane is fixed by a point and a normal vector.
The angle between two lines, or between a line and a plane, comes from a dot product of direction vectors.
Shortest distance between skew lines uses the scalar triple product.

formulas.name: Plane
formulas.expr: ax + by + cz + d = 0, normal (a, b, c)

example: The plane through (1, 2, 3) with normal (2, −1, 4) is 2(x − 1) − (y − 2) + 4(z − 3) = 0.
mistakes: Using direction ratios as if they were unit vectors.
Confusing the normal of a plane with a direction along it.

title: Measures of dispersion
subject: Mathematics
summary: Dispersion measures how spread out a data set is: range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation.
points: Range is the largest value minus the smallest and uses only two observations.
Mean deviation averages the absolute deviations from a central value such as the mean or median.
Variance averages the squared deviations; standard deviation is its square root and has the same units as the data.
The coefficient of variation, standard deviation divided by mean, compares spread across data sets with different units.
example: For 2, 4, 6, 8 the mean is 5, variance is 5 and standard deviation is about 2.24.
mistakes: Forgetting to square deviations before averaging.
Mixing the population and sample formulas.

title: Mathematical reasoning
subject: Mathematics
summary: Mathematical reasoning studies statements, logical connectives and the validity of arguments.
points: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both.
Connectives 'and', 'or', 'if–then' and 'if and only if' combine statements, and their truth depends on the truth of the parts.
A statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent; the converse need not be true.
Quantifiers 'for all' and 'there exists' change the meaning of a statement and its negation.

formulas.name: Implication
formulas.expr: p → q is false only when p is true and q is false

example: "If a number is divisible by 4 then it is even" is true, but its converse "if a number is even then it is divisible by 4" is false.
mistakes: Treating the converse as equivalent to the original.
Negating 'for all' as 'for all not'.

title: Principle of mathematical induction
subject: Mathematics
summary: Mathematical induction proves a statement for all natural numbers by proving a base case and then that truth at n implies truth at n + 1.
points: The base case is usually n = 1 and must be verified directly.
The induction hypothesis assumes the statement for n = k, and the induction step proves it for k + 1.
Both steps are needed: without the base case the chain never starts.
It is a proof technique for statements indexed by natural numbers, not a way to discover formulas.
example: To prove 1 + 3 + … + (2n − 1) = n², the base case n = 1 holds and adding 2k + 1 gives (k + 1)².
mistakes: Skipping the base case.
Assuming the result for all n instead of only n = k.

title: Mechanical properties of solids
subject: Physics
summary: Solids resist deformation because of interatomic forces; stress and strain describe that deformation and the elastic moduli relate them.
points: Stress is force per unit area and strain is the fractional change in dimension; both are needed to compare materials.
Within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law).
Young's modulus applies to stretching, bulk modulus to volume change and shear modulus to shape change.
Beyond the yield point a material deforms permanently, and past the breaking point it fractures.
example: A steel wire of length 2 m stretches 1 mm under load: strain = 1×10⁻³/2 = 5×10⁻⁴.
mistakes: Forgetting that strain has no units.
Using the original length instead of the change in length.

title: Mechanical properties of fluids
subject: Physics
summary: Fluids exert pressure in all directions and their flow is described by continuity, Bernoulli's principle and viscosity.
points: Pressure at depth h is P = P₀ + ρgh, independent of the shape of the container.
An ideal fluid is incompressible and non-viscous; its flow obeys the continuity equation A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
Bernoulli's principle states that where speed is high, pressure is low along a streamline.
Surface tension and capillarity come from cohesive forces at a liquid surface; viscosity resists relative flow.
example: Water flowing from a wide pipe into a narrow one speeds up, and its pressure falls — the basis of a sprayer.
mistakes: Applying Bernoulli across turbulent or viscous flow.
Thinking pressure depends on the amount of liquid rather than depth.

title: Thermal properties of matter
subject: Physics
summary: Heat changes temperature, dimensions and phase; calorimetry and the three modes of heat transfer describe those changes.
points: Linear expansion is ΔL = LαΔT, with area and volume expansion using 2α and 3α.
Specific heat capacity is the heat needed per unit mass per degree; water's is unusually high.
Latent heat is absorbed or released at constant temperature during a phase change.
Conduction needs a medium, convection moves the medium, and radiation needs no medium at all.
example: Melting 100 g of ice at 0 °C needs Q = 0.1 × 3.34×10⁵ = 3.34×10⁴ J.
mistakes: Using Q = mcΔT during a phase change.
Forgetting that area expansion uses 2α.

title: Kinetic theory of gases
subject: Physics
summary: Kinetic theory explains gas pressure and temperature as the average effect of countless molecular collisions.
points: Pressure comes from molecules hitting the walls and changing momentum.
Absolute temperature is proportional to the average translational kinetic energy of molecules.
The ideal gas law follows from the theory: PV = nRT, with R the universal gas constant.
Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature when molecular volume and attraction matter.
example: At 300 K the rms speed of oxygen (M = 0.032 kg/mol) is about 483 m/s.
mistakes: Using degrees Celsius in the gas law.
Assuming molecules have the same speed rather than a distribution.

title: Electric charges and fields
subject: Physics
summary: Stationary charges create electric fields, and the field at a point is the force a unit positive charge would feel there.
points: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract with a force given by Coulomb's law.
Electric field lines start on positive and end on negative charges and never cross.
A dipole consists of equal and opposite charges separated by a distance and has a dipole moment p = q × 2a.
Gauss's law relates the flux through a closed surface to the charge enclosed, and simplifies symmetric problems.
example: Two 1 μC charges 1 m apart repel with F = 9×10⁹ × 10⁻¹² = 9×10⁻³ N.
mistakes: Using the distance between surfaces instead of between charge centres.
Forgetting that field is a vector and must be added vectorially.

title: Electrostatic potential and capacitance
subject: Physics
summary: Electric potential is potential energy per unit charge, and a capacitor stores charge and energy in an electric field.
points: Potential is a scalar, so potentials add directly while fields add as vectors.
The potential difference between two points is the work done per unit charge moving between them.
Capacitance is C = Q/V; for a parallel plate capacitor C = ε₀A/d, increased by a dielectric.
Capacitors in series share charge, in parallel share voltage; energy stored is ½CV².
example: A 2 μF capacitor charged to 100 V stores ½ × 2×10⁻⁶ × 10⁴ = 0.01 J.
mistakes: Adding capacitor voltages in series without checking charge.
Treating potential as a vector.

title: Moving charges and magnetism
subject: Physics
summary: A moving charge or a current creates a magnetic field, and a magnetic field exerts a force on moving charges and current-carrying wires.
points: The force on a moving charge is F = qvB sin θ, perpendicular to both velocity and field.
Biot–Savart law gives the field of a current element; Ampere's circuital law handles symmetric current distributions.
A current loop behaves as a magnetic dipole with moment m = NIA.
A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform field travels in a circle of radius r = mv/qB.

formulas.name: Field at centre of a loop

example: An electron at 10⁷ m/s in a 0.01 T field moves in a circle of radius about 5.7 mm.
mistakes: Forgetting the sin θ factor when velocity is parallel to the field.
Using the loop radius instead of diameter in the field formula.

title: Magnetism and matter
subject: Physics
summary: Materials respond to magnetic fields in different ways depending on how their atomic dipoles align.
points: Diamagnetic materials are weakly repelled, paramagnetic weakly attracted and ferromagnetic strongly attracted.
Ferromagnetism comes from aligned domains that persist after the field is removed, producing permanent magnets.
The earth's magnetic field behaves like a tilted dipole and its poles drift over time.
Susceptibility measures how strongly a material is magnetised by an applied field.
example: Soft iron is used in transformer cores because its narrow hysteresis loop loses little energy per cycle.
mistakes: Thinking diamagnetism needs a permanent magnet.
Confusing magnetic field B with magnetising field H.

title: Alternating current
subject: Physics
summary: An alternating current changes direction periodically, and inductors and capacitors shift the phase between voltage and current.
points: The rms value of a sinusoidal current is peak value divided by √2.
Inductive reactance X_L = ωL rises with frequency; capacitive reactance X_C = 1/ωC falls with frequency.
At resonance in a series LCR circuit X_L = X_C, impedance is minimum and current is maximum.
A transformer changes voltage using mutual induction and loses energy through copper, eddy-current and hysteresis losses.
example: A 50 Hz supply with L = 0.1 H gives X_L = 2π×50×0.1 ≈ 31.4 Ω.
mistakes: Adding reactances arithmetically to resistance.
Using peak instead of rms values in power calculations.

title: Electromagnetic waves
subject: Physics
summary: Accelerating charges produce electromagnetic waves: oscillating electric and magnetic fields travelling perpendicular to each other.
points: E and B are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation; the wave is transverse.
All electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum and slow down in a medium.
The spectrum runs from radio waves through microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-rays to gamma rays.
Displacement current explains how a changing electric field acts as a source of magnetic field.
example: A radio station at 100 MHz broadcasts a wavelength λ = 3×10⁸/10⁸ = 3 m.
mistakes: Saying electromagnetic waves need a medium.
Mixing up the order of the spectrum.

title: Wave optics
subject: Physics
summary: Wave optics treats light as a wave and explains interference, diffraction and polarisation, which ray optics cannot.
points: In Young's double slit experiment, bright fringes occur where path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.
Fringe width is β = λD/d, so it grows with wavelength and screen distance and shrinks with slit separation.
Diffraction at a single slit gives a central maximum twice as wide as the side maxima.
Polarisation shows light is transverse; reflected light is partly polarised at Brewster's angle.
example: With λ = 600 nm, D = 1 m and d = 0.6 mm the fringe width is 1 mm.
mistakes: Using the double-slit formula for a single slit.
Forgetting to convert nanometres to metres.

title: Nuclei and radioactivity
subject: Physics
summary: The nucleus is held together by the strong force; unstable nuclei decay by alpha, beta or gamma emission.
points: Nuclear radius grows as R = R₀A^(1/3), so density is nearly the same for all nuclei.
Mass defect converts to binding energy through E = mc², and binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron.
Radioactive decay is random and exponential, described by N = N₀e^(−λt).
Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay, and activity is measured in becquerel.
Fission splits heavy nuclei and fusion joins light ones, both releasing energy.
example: Carbon-14 with a 5,730-year half-life has 25% left after 11,460 years.
mistakes: Treating decay as predictable for a single nucleus.
Mixing up half-life with mean life.
